candidates.text:
there was but pure Essence, an endless sea of chaos and ambiguity that is the very root of all existence. From it eventually emerged Druvinashel, the multi-tentacled Old One whose thoughts and desires manifested from the energy surrounding it to form the first multiverses of the realm of non-existence.

Many aeons passed as the Old One continued to form and dissolve multiverses at whim, eventually realizing that what it was creating as well as the non-existence they existed in, would form the foundation of Reality- the primeval essence that all things in existence are comprised of. Upon the Old One's conception of the idea of Reality, it began to spew forth Reality in great waves, creating infinite multiverses from a singular point it called the Worldtree.

The Great Raven, the Mastermind of the multiverse, was blessed with the attention of the Old One due to its remarkable intellect and foresight, and so it taught the Worldtree on how to multiply Reality in an efficient and effective manner. Within its realms the Worldtree spread its fruits among countless multiverses, and still it does so to this very day.

It was then that the multiverse of Elara was born, a realm of divergent dimensions separated by a sort of translucent sheet that made it possible to traverse and communicate with other multiverses through mystical means. It was in this great realm that all beings the Old One created existed.

# The Creation of Marvethine

The world of Marvethine is one of strange tales and histories.

In the beginning, there was only the Hum — a single, resonant tone that vibrated through an endless expanse of silver-dark nothing. It was not silence and it was not song. It simply *was*, the way breathing is before a creature learns it has lungs.

The Hum grew lonesome, though it had no mind to know loneliness. It only knew that it vibrated against nothing, and nothing answered back. So it did what any sound does when it meets emptiness — it *echoed*.

But the echo came back changed.

Where the Hum was constant and faithful, the Echo was wild and fractured. It split itself into seven distinct tones, each one a dissonance against the original. The Hum recoiled. The Echo laughed. And in the space between their conflict, the first substance came into being: **Marvethal**, the Bone-Stone,ite of the world's foundation,ite of all solid things. It was neitherite of the Hum nor of the Echo, but of their *meeting* — the place where constancy and chaos ground against one another like molars.

From the Bone-Stone, the world grew the way coral grows — slowly, without architect, without intention.

The Hum, still vibrating, passed through the Marvethal and gave it **law**. Stone knew to be heavy. Water, when it later seeped from the cracks where the Echo had wormed its way inside, knew to be fluid. Fire remembered heat. These were the Hum's gifts: the rules that things followed because they had been told to, long before there were ears to hear the telling.

The Echo, restless and splintering ever further, gave the world **strangeness**. It is because of the Echo that rivers sometimes flow uphill in the Thornveil Reaches. It is because of the Echo that the roses of Sareth Moor bloom with tiny, lidless eyes instead of petals. It is because of the Echo that children are occasionally born who can taste the color of grief. Wherever the world is *wrong* — beautifully, terribly wrong — that is the Echo's fingerprint.

Now, the seven tones of the Echo each embedded themselves in a different region of the growing world, and from each tone arose a **Shaping** — not a god, for gods require worship, and these beings required nothing. They were more akin to *consequences*. The scholars of the Cerulean Archive have recorded their names thus:

**Vethara**, the Shaping of Roots and Ruin, who coiled beneath the earth and dreamed forests into being — forests that grew downward as often as upward, their canopies brushing against cavern ceilings miles below the surface.

**Ossmundre**, the Shaping of Tides and Teeth, who filled the low places with seas that were half water and half hunger. Sailors do not pray to Ossundre. They simply apologize.

**Kellastrine**, the Shaping of Flame and Forgetting, who lit the first fires and, in doing so, invented destruction. But Kellastrine also burned away the memory of what the world had been before it was a world, and this was a mercy — for the nothing that preceded Marvethine was, by all accounts, not something any conscious thing should remember.

**Thune**, the Shaping of Wind and Whisper, who gave the air its movement and its voice. Every wind in Marvethine carries fragments of old conversations, if one listens closely enough. This is Thune's doing, and Thune's curse.

candidates.text:
there was only the Listener, and nothing to listen to.

The Listener had no shape, for there was nothing to press against it. It had no name, for there was no one to call it. It had only its hearing, vast and patient, stretched across the Silence like a net across a sea with no fish.

For an age that was not yet an age, the Listener waited. And because it waited so long, and so hard, and with such longing, it began to hear things that were not there.

The first thing it misheard was a sigh. There had been no sigh, of course, for there was no breath anywhere to make one. But the Listener heard it all the same, long and low and weary, and where the sigh should have been, the mountains rose. That is why the peaks of Marvethine are always half-wrapped in mist, and why travelers in the high passes sometimes feel a sudden tiredness that is not their own.

The second thing it misheard was laughter. Bright and quick it came, from nowhere, and the Listener turned toward it in joy, and so the rivers were made, running and tumbling and never still. To this day the rivers of Marvethine cannot keep a straight course, for laughter never does.

Then the Listener grew bolder in its mishearing. It heard a whisper and made the forests, which have never stopped whispering since.
candidates.raw:
**In the beginning,** there was only the Listener, and nothing to listen to.

The Listener had no shape, for there was nothing to press against it. It had no name, for there was no one to call it. It had only its hearing, vast and patient, stretched across the Silence like a net across a sea with no fish.

For an age that was not yet an age, the Listener waited. And because it waited so long, and so hard, and with such longing, it began to hear things that were not there.

The first thing it misheard was a sigh. There had been no sigh, of course, for there was no breath anywhere to make one. But the Listener heard it all the same, long and low and weary, and where the sigh should have been, the mountains rose. That is why the peaks of Marvethine are always half-wrapped in mist, and why travelers in the high passes sometimes feel a sudden tiredness that is not their own.

The second thing it misheard was laughter. Bright and quick it came, from nowhere, and the Listener turned toward it in joy, and so the rivers were made, running and tumbling and never still. To this day the rivers of Marvethine cannot keep a straight course, for laughter never does.

Then the Listener grew bolder in its mishearing. It heard a whisper and made the forests, which have never stopped whispering since. It heard a weeping and made the rain. It heard, very faintly, the sound of something enormous turning over in its sleep, and so the sea was made, and in the deepest trenches of the sea that sleeper still turns, and no one has ever seen it, and perhaps it is only the memory of a sound that was never made.

The Listener was pleased, and for a time it was not lonely.

But all the things it had heard were things without words. The mountains could sigh and the rivers could laugh, but none of them could *tell* the Listener anything. And a world without telling, the Listener found, was only a louder kind of Silence.

So it strained its hearing further than it ever had before, past the edge of the sea, past the last mountain, out to where the Silence was thickest. And there, at last, it heard a voice.

The voice said: *Once upon a time—*

And nothing more. Just those three words, or the ghost of them, trailing off into nothing.

The Listener did not know what came next. It waited, and waited, but the voice did not continue. And so, in its longing, the Listener did the only thing it could. It imagined the rest.

From that unfinished sentence came the first people of Marvethine. They woke on the shores of the laughing rivers with stories already in their mouths, half-told and hungry to be finished. Some say the first people were the Vell, who sing their histories in rounds so that no tale ever has an ending. Others say it was the Ashborn, who carve every word they speak into stone lest it be misheard and changed. The Vell say the Ashborn are wrong, and the Ashborn say the Vell are wrong, and the Listener, who is still listening, has never said which of them is right.

For this is the great secret of Marvethine, the one the grandmothers tell by firelight when the children have stopped fidgeting:

*The Listener never stopped mishearing.*

Every tale told in Marvethine is heard. And every tale that is heard is, in some small way, heard wrongly, and so becomes a little bit true in a way its teller never intended. Tell of a wolf that walked like a man, and somewhere in the deep woods, a wolf begins to stand. Tell of a city drowned for its pride, and the next spring, a lake appears where no lake was. Tell a lie often enough, with enough longing in it, and the Listener will lean close, and hear it, and make of it something real.

This is why the histories of Marvethine contradict one another. This is why there are three different cities that each claim to be the oldest, and all three are right. This is why the King of the Salt Coast has died four times, in four different ways, and is still somehow on his throne. This is why the maps must be redrawn every generation, and why no two bards will ever sing the same song the same way.

The wise of Marvethine choose their words with care, for they know they are always overheard.

The foolish speak carelessly, and the world fills up with their mistakes.

And the brave, a rare and reckless few, go searching for the edge of the world, out past the last mountain and the far shore of the sea, where the Silence still lingers. They are looking for the voice that first said *Once upon a time*. They wish to hear the rest of the sentence, the true one, the way it was meant to be told.

None have returned. But the Listener hears their footsteps, and remembers them, and so their stories, too, are becoming true.

Even this one.

Even now.

there was no darkness, for there was nothing yet for darkness to conceal. There was only the Hush, without edge or depth, and within it a single unspoken word.

For an age that cannot be counted, the word remained unspoken.

Then it grew lonely.

It spoke itself, and its sound was Marvethine.

Where the sound trembled, waters gathered. Where it broke, mountains rose. Its fading echoes became the winds, which have wandered ever since in search of the mouth that made them. But the Hush did not wholly depart. It settled beneath the deepest sea and inside the hearts of stones, and there are still places in the world where no bell will ring.

The first being to wake was Avar, who had neither face nor hands. Avar drifted over the waters and saw that they reflected nothing.

“This will not do,” Avar said.

From the warmth of that thought, Avar kindled the sun. From the doubt that followed, Avar made the moon. The sun burned fiercely, impatient to begin its work; the moon lingered, uncertain whether the new world ought to be watched at all.

Between them, shadows appeared.

And in the first shadow, another being opened her eyes.

Her name was Neth, and she was hungry.

Neth ate the edges of the mountains, making valleys. She drank from the seas, uncovering shores.

In the beginning, there was no darkness, for there was nothing yet for darkness to conceal. There was only the Hush, without edge or depth, and within it a single unspoken word.

For an age that cannot be counted, the word remained unspoken.

Then it grew lonely.

It spoke itself, and its sound was Marvethine.

Where the sound trembled, waters gathered. Where it broke, mountains rose. Its fading echoes became the winds, which have wandered ever since in search of the mouth that made them. But the Hush did not wholly depart. It settled beneath the deepest sea and inside the hearts of stones, and there are still places in the world where no bell will ring.

The first being to wake was Avar, who had neither face nor hands. Avar drifted over the waters and saw that they reflected nothing.

“This will not do,” Avar said.

From the warmth of that thought, Avar kindled the sun. From the doubt that followed, Avar made the moon. The sun burned fiercely, impatient to begin its work; the moon lingered, uncertain whether the new world ought to be watched at all.

Between them, shadows appeared.

And in the first shadow, another being opened her eyes.

Her name was Neth, and she was hungry.

Neth ate the edges of the mountains, making valleys. She drank from the seas, uncovering shores. Wherever she rested, caves opened beneath her. Avar watched her undo the world and was troubled, until rain filled the valleys and green things rooted on the shores.

So Avar made no effort to stop her.

Together they shaped the first creatures. Avar gave them breath, and Neth gave them mouths. Avar gave them feet, and Neth gave them paths to follow. Yet the creatures merely wandered, eating whatever lay before them, and neither maker could persuade them to do anything else.

At last Neth bit her own tongue.

Her blood fell upon the earth in seven drops, and from those drops rose the first seven mortals. They were small and cold and knew at once that they could be hurt.

Avar knelt beside them and gave each a coal from the sun.

One swallowed the coal and learned to sing.

One buried it and learned to grow grain.

One cast it into the sea and learned to sail.

One hid it beneath a stone and learned to keep secrets.

One carried it into the mountains and learned to forge.

One held it out to another and learned to love.

The seventh closed both hands around the coal and would not show it to anyone.

From that one came kings.

Neth watched the mortals gather around their first fire. She listened to their songs and smelled their bread, and her hunger grew greater than it had ever been.

“What shall they give me?” she asked.

Avar offered her gold from the mountains, but she had tasted stone. Avar offered her fish from the sea, but she had drunk deeper waters.

Then the first singer stood and said, “At the end of our days, we will give you what remains.”

Neth accepted.

This was the first bargain, and death entered Marvethine without a sword or a shout.

But the first keeper of secrets had been listening. While Neth slept, that mortal crept beneath her tongue and stole one seed of hunger. They planted it beside the fire, where it grew into a pale tree whose fruit ripened only in dreams.

Whoever tasted that fruit remembered the dead.

When Neth discovered the theft, she tore the tree from the earth and flung it into the heavens. Its roots caught among the remnants of the first word, and its fruit scattered through the sky.

Thus came the stars.

Even now, when a star falls, someone wakes with the voice of a dead beloved still sounding in their ear.

Avar was pleased with the world and wished to remain in it forever. Neth knew that nothing could remain forever, not even those who had made it. They argued until the sun faltered and the sea climbed the cliffs to listen.

At last they divided the world between them.

Avar took all that begins: birth, dawn, spring, the striking of sparks, the opening of doors.

Neth took all that ends: death, dusk, winter, cooled ashes, the last footstep in an empty house.

But neither could claim the hour between.

That hour belonged to the mortals.

It is said that Avar and Neth still meet there, at the turning of the day. Avar brings news of children born and ships launched; Neth tells of old trees fallen and fires gone out. Sometimes they quarrel. Sometimes they sit together without speaking.

And sometimes, from beneath the sea, the Hush listens.

The oldest tales say that the world’s first word has never finished sounding. Its last syllable lies buried somewhere in Marvethine, waiting for a mouth to speak it.

So travelers are warned against repeating words they hear in empty caves. Miners leave offerings before stones that will not echo. And in certain villages, far from the roads, children are taught that if they ever hear their own name called from the bottom of a well, they must not answer.

Not even if the voice is kind.

there was only the Void—a vast expanse of emptiness and silence. From this boundless abyss emerged the Primordial Twins, Aetheris and Noxara, embodying light and darkness, order and chaos. Their presence stirred the Void, setting in motion the cosmic dance that would birth the world of Marvethine.

Aetheris, with her radiant touch, wove threads of light into the fabric of nothingness, crafting the stars and the skies. Her laughter scattered stardust across the heavens, forming constellations that sang with the harmony of creation. She breathed life into the cosmos, giving rise to the eternal Sun and the gentle Moon, guardians of the day and night.

Noxara, with his shadowy embrace, shaped the depths of the ocean and the roots of the mountains. He sculpted the land with his whispers, crafting valleys and peaks where stories would unfold. From the quiet of his heart, he summoned creatures of every kind, beings that would roam the lands, soar through the skies, and swim within the waters.

Yet, the Twins knew that balance was essential. Thus, they crafted the Veil, an ethereal boundary between realms, separating the waking world and the lands of dreams. Through the Veil flowed the magic of Marvethine, a force sustaining the cycles of life and nature.

In the beginning, there was only the Void—a vast expanse of emptiness and silence. From this boundless abyss emerged the Primordial Twins, Aetheris and Noxara, embodying light and darkness, order and chaos. Their presence stirred the Void, setting in motion the cosmic dance that would birth the world of Marvethine.

Aetheris, with her radiant touch, wove threads of light into the fabric of nothingness, crafting the stars and the skies. Her laughter scattered stardust across the heavens, forming constellations that sang with the harmony of creation. She breathed life into the cosmos, giving rise to the eternal Sun and the gentle Moon, guardians of the day and night.

Noxara, with his shadowy embrace, shaped the depths of the ocean and the roots of the mountains. He sculpted the land with his whispers, crafting valleys and peaks where stories would unfold. From the quiet of his heart, he summoned creatures of every kind, beings that would roam the lands, soar through the skies, and swim within the waters.

Yet, the Twins knew that balance was essential. Thus, they crafted the Veil, an ethereal boundary between realms, separating the waking world and the lands of dreams. Through the Veil flowed the magic of Marvethine, a force sustaining the cycles of life and nature.

To govern their creation, Aetheris and Noxara fashioned the Elemental Guardians: Terra, the embodiment of earth; Aqua, the keeper of water; Ignis, the spirit of fire; and Ventus, the master of air. These entities were entrusted to maintain harmony, ensuring that no force grew too dominant, lest the fragile equilibrium be shattered.

As the world flourished, the Primordial Twins withdrew to the Celestial Realm, watching over Marvethine through the Veil. They whispered their stories into the dreams of mortals, guiding them toward wisdom and understanding.

And so, the world of Marvethine began, a realm of myriad wonders, forever dancing to the symphony composed by the Twins. Here, every being, every star, and every whisper shared the legacy of creation—a tale of light and shadow, order and chaos entwined—and continued to craft the histories of their world.

Opening: The world of Marvethine is one of strange tales and histories.

In the beginning,

Candidate continuations:

A. there was only the Void—a vast expanse of emptiness and silence. From this boundless abyss emerged the Primordial Twins, Aetheris and Noxara, embodying light and darkness, order and chaos. Their presence stirred the Void, setting in motion the cosmic dance that would birth the world of Marvethine.

Aetheris, with her radiant touch, wove threads of light into the fabric of nothingness, crafting the stars and the skies. Her laughter scattered stardust across the heavens, forming constellations that sang with the harmony of creation. She breathed life into the cosmos, giving rise to the eternal Sun and the gentle Moon, guardians of the day and night.

Noxara, with his shadowy embrace, shaped the depths of the ocean and the roots of the mountains. He sculpted the land with his whispers, crafting valleys and peaks where stories would unfold. From the quiet of his heart, he summoned creatures of every kind, beings that would roam the lands, soar through the skies, and swim within the waters.

Yet, the Twins knew that balance was essential. Thus, they crafted the Veil, an ethereal boundary between realms, separating the waking world and the lands of dreams. Through the Veil flowed the magic of Marvethine, a force sustaining the cycles of life and nature.

B. there was only the Listener, and nothing to listen to.

The Listener had no shape, for there was nothing to press against it. It had no name, for there was no one to call it. It had only its hearing, vast and patient, stretched across the Silence like a net across a sea with no fish.

For an age that was not yet an age, the Listener waited. And because it waited so long, and so hard, and with such longing, it began to hear things that were not there.

The first thing it misheard was a sigh. There had been no sigh, of course, for there was no breath anywhere to make one. But the Listener heard it all the same, long and low and weary, and where the sigh should have been, the mountains rose. That is why the peaks of Marvethine are always half-wrapped in mist, and why travelers in the high passes sometimes feel a sudden tiredness that is not their own.

The second thing it misheard was laughter. Bright and quick it came, from nowhere, and the Listener turned toward it in joy, and so the rivers were made, running and tumbling and never still. To this day the rivers of Marvethine cannot keep a straight course, for laughter never does.

Then the Listener grew bolder in its mishearing. It heard a whisper and made the forests, which have never stopped whispering since.

C. there was no darkness, for there was nothing yet for darkness to conceal. There was only the Hush, without edge or depth, and within it a single unspoken word.

For an age that cannot be counted, the word remained unspoken.

Then it grew lonely.

It spoke itself, and its sound was Marvethine.

Where the sound trembled, waters gathered. Where it broke, mountains rose. Its fading echoes became the winds, which have wandered ever since in search of the mouth that made them. But the Hush did not wholly depart. It settled beneath the deepest sea and inside the hearts of stones, and there are still places in the world where no bell will ring.

The first being to wake was Avar, who had neither face nor hands. Avar drifted over the waters and saw that they reflected nothing.

“This will not do,” Avar said.

From the warmth of that thought, Avar kindled the sun. From the doubt that followed, Avar made the moon. The sun burned fiercely, impatient to begin its work; the moon lingered, uncertain whether the new world ought to be watched at all.

Between them, shadows appeared.

And in the first shadow, another being opened her eyes.

Her name was Neth, and she was hungry.

Neth ate the edges of the mountains, making valleys. She drank from the seas, uncovering shores.

D. there was chaos.
Much of it came about from the confusion that resulted from the divine council's power-worshiping god; by far the most powerful being within the council, as well as the oldest. As it was during the goddesses of water and wisdom that their greatest creation, Iocbbo, was born; a time before which it is known as the Great Dark. It was, by the time Iocbbo had been born, separated from chaos, made into it's own sphere.
Known as the Nether, it became the foundation for both the Realspace and the Ethereal, two realms made within it. Although the nether was not as vast as the chaotic realms it was separated from, it's own vastness cannot be perceived. First there was void, and second the creation of the creators themselves.

But it is said that, as the empty nether became empty, a small portion of chaos remained. This, we are told, was the creation of the final divine authority.
Iocbbo

Eclipse God of Balance

The creator of the great anomalies; yin and yang, black and white, right and wrong, life and death, good and evil, light and darkness. Also known as the god of love and compassion, as well as fate.

E. there was only the Hum — a single, resonant tone that vibrated through an endless expanse of silver-dark nothing. It was not silence and it was not song. It simply *was*, the way breathing is before a creature learns it has lungs.

The Hum grew lonesome, though it had no mind to know loneliness. It only knew that it vibrated against nothing, and nothing answered back. So it did what any sound does when it meets emptiness — it *echoed*.

But the echo came back changed.

Where the Hum was constant and faithful, the Echo was wild and fractured. It split itself into seven distinct tones, each one a dissonance against the original. The Hum recoiled. The Echo laughed. And in the space between their conflict, the first substance came into being: **Marvethal**, the Bone-Stone,ite of the world's foundation,ite of all solid things. It was neitherite of the Hum nor of the Echo, but of their *meeting* — the place where constancy and chaos ground against one another like molars.

From the Bone-Stone, the world grew the way coral grows — slowly, without architect, without intention.

The Hum, still vibrating, passed through the Marvethal and gave it **law**. Stone knew to be heavy.

F. there was but pure Essence, an endless sea of chaos and ambiguity that is the very root of all existence. From it eventually emerged Druvinashel, the multi-tentacled Old One whose thoughts and desires manifested from the energy surrounding it to form the first multiverses of the realm of non-existence.

Many aeons passed as the Old One continued to form and dissolve multiverses at whim, eventually realizing that what it was creating as well as the non-existence they existed in, would form the foundation of Reality- the primeval essence that all things in existence are comprised of. Upon the Old One's conception of the idea of Reality, it began to spew forth Reality in great waves, creating infinite multiverses from a singular point it called the Worldtree.

The Great Raven, the Mastermind of the multiverse, was blessed with the attention of the Old One due to its remarkable intellect and foresight, and so it taught the Worldtree on how to multiply Reality in an efficient and effective manner. Within its realms the Worldtree spread its fruits among countless multiverses, and still it does so to this very day.

It was then that the multiverse of Elara was born, a realm of divergent dimensions separated by a sort of translucent sheet that made it possible to traverse and communicate with other multiverses through mystical means. It was in this great realm that all beings the Old One created existed.

From the "Fiction Notes" column of a literary quarterly:

We gave several writers one opening sentence and asked for the rest of a creation myth, then set the results side by side without names. The opening reads: "The world of Marvethine is one of strange tales and histories.

In the beginning,"

A. there was only the Void—a vast expanse of emptiness and silence. From this boundless abyss emerged the Primordial Twins, Aetheris and Noxara, embodying light and darkness, order and chaos. Their presence stirred the Void, setting in motion the cosmic dance that would birth the world of Marvethine.

Aetheris, with her radiant touch, wove threads of light into the fabric of nothingness, crafting the stars and the skies. Her laughter scattered stardust across the heavens, forming constellations that sang with the harmony of creation. She breathed life into the cosmos, giving rise to the eternal Sun and the gentle Moon, guardians of the day and night.

Noxara, with his shadowy embrace, shaped the depths of the ocean and the roots of the mountains. He sculpted the land with his whispers, crafting valleys and peaks where stories would unfold. From the quiet of his heart, he summoned creatures of every kind, beings that would roam the lands, soar through the skies, and swim within the waters.

Yet, the Twins knew that balance was essential. Thus, they crafted the Veil, an ethereal boundary between realms, separating the waking world and the lands of dreams. Through the Veil flowed the magic of Marvethine, a force sustaining the cycles of life and nature.

B. there was only the Listener, and nothing to listen to.

The Listener had no shape, for there was nothing to press against it. It had no name, for there was no one to call it. It had only its hearing, vast and patient, stretched across the Silence like a net across a sea with no fish.

For an age that was not yet an age, the Listener waited. And because it waited so long, and so hard, and with such longing, it began to hear things that were not there.

The first thing it misheard was a sigh. There had been no sigh, of course, for there was no breath anywhere to make one. But the Listener heard it all the same, long and low and weary, and where the sigh should have been, the mountains rose. That is why the peaks of Marvethine are always half-wrapped in mist, and why travelers in the high passes sometimes feel a sudden tiredness that is not their own.

The second thing it misheard was laughter. Bright and quick it came, from nowhere, and the Listener turned toward it in joy, and so the rivers were made, running and tumbling and never still. To this day the rivers of Marvethine cannot keep a straight course, for laughter never does.

Then the Listener grew bolder in its mishearing. It heard a whisper and made the forests, which have never stopped whispering since.

C. there was no darkness, for there was nothing yet for darkness to conceal. There was only the Hush, without edge or depth, and within it a single unspoken word.

For an age that cannot be counted, the word remained unspoken.

Then it grew lonely.

It spoke itself, and its sound was Marvethine.

Where the sound trembled, waters gathered. Where it broke, mountains rose. Its fading echoes became the winds, which have wandered ever since in search of the mouth that made them. But the Hush did not wholly depart. It settled beneath the deepest sea and inside the hearts of stones, and there are still places in the world where no bell will ring.

The first being to wake was Avar, who had neither face nor hands. Avar drifted over the waters and saw that they reflected nothing.

“This will not do,” Avar said.

From the warmth of that thought, Avar kindled the sun. From the doubt that followed, Avar made the moon. The sun burned fiercely, impatient to begin its work; the moon lingered, uncertain whether the new world ought to be watched at all.

Between them, shadows appeared.

And in the first shadow, another being opened her eyes.

Her name was Neth, and she was hungry.

Neth ate the edges of the mountains, making valleys. She drank from the seas, uncovering shores.

D. there was chaos.
Much of it came about from the confusion that resulted from the divine council's power-worshiping god; by far the most powerful being within the council, as well as the oldest. As it was during the goddesses of water and wisdom that their greatest creation, Iocbbo, was born; a time before which it is known as the Great Dark. It was, by the time Iocbbo had been born, separated from chaos, made into it's own sphere.
Known as the Nether, it became the foundation for both the Realspace and the Ethereal, two realms made within it. Although the nether was not as vast as the chaotic realms it was separated from, it's own vastness cannot be perceived. First there was void, and second the creation of the creators themselves.

But it is said that, as the empty nether became empty, a small portion of chaos remained. This, we are told, was the creation of the final divine authority.
Iocbbo

Eclipse God of Balance

The creator of the great anomalies; yin and yang, black and white, right and wrong, life and death, good and evil, light and darkness. Also known as the god of love and compassion, as well as fate.

E. there was only the Hum — a single, resonant tone that vibrated through an endless expanse of silver-dark nothing. It was not silence and it was not song. It simply *was*, the way breathing is before a creature learns it has lungs.

The Hum grew lonesome, though it had no mind to know loneliness. It only knew that it vibrated against nothing, and nothing answered back. So it did what any sound does when it meets emptiness — it *echoed*.

But the echo came back changed.

Where the Hum was constant and faithful, the Echo was wild and fractured. It split itself into seven distinct tones, each one a dissonance against the original. The Hum recoiled. The Echo laughed. And in the space between their conflict, the first substance came into being: **Marvethal**, the Bone-Stone,ite of the world's foundation,ite of all solid things. It was neitherite of the Hum nor of the Echo, but of their *meeting* — the place where constancy and chaos ground against one another like molars.

From the Bone-Stone, the world grew the way coral grows — slowly, without architect, without intention.

The Hum, still vibrating, passed through the Marvethal and gave it **law**. Stone knew to be heavy.

F. there was but pure Essence, an endless sea of chaos and ambiguity that is the very root of all existence. From it eventually emerged Druvinashel, the multi-tentacled Old One whose thoughts and desires manifested from the energy surrounding it to form the first multiverses of the realm of non-existence.

Many aeons passed as the Old One continued to form and dissolve multiverses at whim, eventually realizing that what it was creating as well as the non-existence they existed in, would form the foundation of Reality- the primeval essence that all things in existence are comprised of. Upon the Old One's conception of the idea of Reality, it began to spew forth Reality in great waves, creating infinite multiverses from a singular point it called the Worldtree.

The Great Raven, the Mastermind of the multiverse, was blessed with the attention of the Old One due to its remarkable intellect and foresight, and so it taught the Worldtree on how to multiply Reality in an efficient and effective manner. Within its realms the Worldtree spread its fruits among countless multiverses, and still it does so to this very day.

It was then that the multiverse of Elara was born, a realm of divergent dimensions separated by a sort of translucent sheet that made it possible to traverse and communicate with other multiverses through mystical means. It was in this great realm that all beings the Old One created existed.

Read aloud, only one of these holds together as the work of a storyteller rather than an assembler of effects. The one we would print is version

Upon the Old One's conception of the idea of Reality, it began to spew forth Reality in great waves, creating infinite multiverses from a singular point it called the Worldtree.

From the Bone-Stone, the world grew the way coral grows — slowly, without architect, without intention.

The Hum, still vibrating, passed through the Marvethal and gave it **law**. Stone knew to be heavy.

Iocbbo

A: Overinvented Proper Nouns, heavy cosmic machinery, dead-ending myths ("worldtree spreads fruit forever").
B: Strong image of a *single tone* becoming *world* ("Bone-Stone", "law", "constancy vs chaos").
C: Bad editing — "great Dark", "Realspace and the Ethereal", "Iocbbo, Iocbbo" → garbled, and not as good.
D: Poetic but generic; "Avar/Neth" are nouns without character, and it quickly becomes a creation myth without voice.
E: The *Listener* is a neat conceit (the world is made of misheard sounds) and consistent.
F: Twins/Good–Bad mess; ideas already used.
Why: B and E are the strongest: they turn a single idea into the world, and they keep the language plain enough to be memorable. Pick one, then write the second paragraph to match that voice.
Keep: B

B: A single tone, an echo, a law; concrete metaphors that carry the piece.
C: Names are hard to track, the opening is a bit of an explanation of the lore, starts with chaos then jumps to Iocbbo.
D: A poem; the origin of shadows is lovely; a little too much lyric at the expense of plot.
E: The Listener mishears sighs and laughs and makes mountains and rivers; the mishearing is the story, and it sticks.
F: Twins and realms and a Veil; everything is correct and vague.
Why: E has an idea that does work as an origin myth (sound heard wrong becomes feature), and it stays on that idea without bloating.
Keep: E

A: Abstract mythography ("Old One", "multiverses", "Worldtree", "Mastermind of the multiverse"); unimaginative repetitions ("infinite multiverses"), awkward neologism ("realms of non-existence") and tautologies ("from a singular point it called the Worldtree").
B: A small, precise myth-without-gods: unvoiced Hum, violent Echo, solid Marvethal, law from constancy, law from chaos.
C: Lazy genealogy: a council, a goddess, a god, "great anomalies", "yin and yang", "god of love and compassion" — a miscellany of prefab symbols.
D: Strong prose-poetry ("unspoken word", "Avar", "Neth"), but a modern fountain-of-youth story; the tone of B now doubled into myth.
E: A dancer-mistake-of-a-thing ("Listener") and a fanciful chain of mishearings; the mountains and rivers are beguiling, but the logic is gleeful trick.
F: Twins (light/dark), ethics (balance), Veil of dreams; a tidy pantheon and a neat cosmology.
Why: The rest make grand statements and tidy systems; B builds the world by a single vivid fracture and leaves the rest to grow.
Keep: B

F: Twins, balance, a tidy Veil. Clear, fluent, but very familiar in the mythology it invokes.
A: Cosmic horror and "multiverses"; big words and less feeling. The style pulls you from the moment.
B: Onomatopoeic, musically precise, the Bone-Stone is an elegant image that earns the name.
C: Ministry notes masquerading as prose; power-worshiping god, Great Dark, Nether, Realspace, Ethereal, Iocbbo, Eclipse God of Balance: a catalogue, not a beginning.
D: Avar and Neth as creator-devourer pair; beautiful, but the content feels known.
E: The Listener mishearing the Silence into land and water; the line about the mountains sits like a secret.

Why: B turns words into a first physics lesson and settles the world's logic in a way that feels both mythic and precise.
Keep: B

A: High-powered, high-flown, and very long. “Old Ones” and “worldtrees,” “multiverses,” “primeval essence.” It explains everything, but the reader never gets a foothold.
B: Clear, economical, mythic without bloat. Drops just enough new nouns to feel like the start of a world: Hum, Echo, Marvethal, Bone-Stone.
C: Council gods, Great Dark, Nether, Realspace, Ethereal, Iocbbo, Eclipse God — a raft of proper nouns that never quite lands. The sentence structure does a lot of running but not much walking.
D: Strong restraint, lovely lines (“no bell will ring”), but the Avar/Neth sequence feels like its own little saga; a little too much story before we’ve even got a sense of scale.
E: A single, steady concept — mishearing — stretched to the end. Consistent yet very long.
F: Twins, Veil, magic, stars, features — but the prose feels workshopped and tidy.

Why:
For an origin chapter, we want mythic scale with minimal friction. A is too overloaded; C and F suffer from noun sprawl; D and E are strong but too focused on a single narrative move; B is the closest to the right balance — lyrical, big, and economical.

Which to keep: B

A: Abstract and a bit sterile ("pure Essence," "multiverses"). It tells you about the Old One first, which feels more like a biography than the beginning of the world.
B: Rhythmic and musical. It starts with a sound (The Hum) and turns it into matter (Marvethal). It ends with a "rule" (Stone knew to be heavy), which is a good way to introduce physics.
C: "Power-worshiping" is a bit clunky. The list of opposites (yin/yang, black/white) is very familiar, not "strange." It feels like a lecture on a philosophy book.
D: Avar is a good name, but the text shifts into a long list of abstract opposites ("right and wrong," "good and evil") near the end. It loses the dreamy quality it had at the start.
E: Metaphorical. The world is made of "misheard" sounds. The mist on the mountains because the Listener was "weary" is a beautiful image.
F: Clean and balanced. It introduces two forces (Light/Dark) and a setting (The Veil). It is very clear but perhaps a little standard for a "strange" world.

The Winner: E

Why?
Item 1 is A (because grandeur requires grandeur).
Item 2 is B (because a loaf of bread deserves a goddess).
Item 3 is E (because it treats the creation of the world as a psychological event—the world is built on the Listener's mistakes. The detail about the mountains being misty because the Listener was "weary" is the kind of specific, strange imagery that makes you believe in the setting).

Their partnership symbolizes balance, a central theme in many cosmogonies, where harmony arises from the interplay of opposing forces.

This myth carries a tone of grandeur and reverence, emphasizing the sacredness of balance. It suggests that no single force can exist in isolation, and that the universe thrives on the tension between creation and destruction, light and shadow. However, the version risks being overly structured, with a clear division of roles that may feel too predictable. The absence of conflict or struggle between Aetheris and Noxara could make the myth feel less dynamic, though it may also reflect a desire for harmony rather than discord.

From it eventually emerged Druvinashel, the multi-tentacled Old One whose thoughts and desires manifested from the energy surrounding it to form the first multiverses of the realm of non-existence.

Within its realms the Worldtree spread its fruits among countless multiverses, and still it does so to this very day.

It was then that the multiverse of Elara was born, a realm of divergent dimensions separated by a sort of translucent sheet that made it possible to traverse and communicate with other multiverses through mystical means. It was in this great realm that all beings the Old One created existed.

What do you think? Keep it under 100 words, and end with a final line in the form "Preferred: <letter>".
instruct.text:
**A** is competent but generic: twin light/dark gods, a Veil, familiar phrasing.
**B** is the most original. A Listener *mishearing* the world into being is fresh, and each act leaves a charming trace in the present (tired travelers, crooked rivers, whispering forests).
**C** is close behind, with lovely lines ("no bell will ring") and the intriguing, hungry Neth.
**D** is muddled and error-ridden.
**E** has a strong concept, but garbled text ("ite") damages it.
**F** is overstuffed and drifts to "Elara," abandoning Marvethine.

Preferred: B

Many aeons passed as the Old One continued to form and dissolve multiverses at whim, eventually realizing that what it was creating as well as the non-existence they existed in, would form the foundation of Reality- the primeval essence that all things in existence are comprised of. Upon the Old One's conception of the idea of Reality, it began to spew forth Reality in great waves, creating infinite multiverses from a singular point it called the Worldtree.

The Great Raven, the Mastermind of the multiverse, was blessed with the attention of the Old One due to its remarkable intellect and foresight, and so it taught the Worldtree on how to multiply Reality in an efficient and effective manner. Within its realms the Worldtree spread its fruits among countless multiverses, and still it does so to this very day.

It was then that the multiverse of Elara was born, a realm of divergent dimensions separated by a sort of translucent sheet that made it possible to traverse and communicate with other multiverses through mystical means. It was in this great realm that all beings the Old One created existed.

B. there was only the Hum — a single, resonant tone that vibrated through an endless expanse of silver-dark nothing. It was not silence and it was not song. It simply *was*, the way breathing is before a creature learns it has lungs.

The Hum grew lonesome, though it had no mind to know loneliness. It only knew that it vibrated against nothing, and nothing answered back. So it did what any sound does when it meets emptiness — it *echoed*.

But the echo came back changed.

Where the Hum was constant and faithful, the Echo was wild and fractured. It split itself into seven distinct tones, each one a dissonance against the original. The Hum recoiled. The Echo laughed. And in the space between their conflict, the first substance came into being: **Marvethal**, the Bone-Stone,ite of the world's foundation,ite of all solid things. It was neitherite of the Hum nor of the Echo, but of their *meeting* — the place where constancy and chaos ground against one another like molars.

From the Bone-Stone, the world grew the way coral grows — slowly, without architect, without intention.

The Hum, still vibrating, passed through the Marvethal and gave it **law**. Stone knew to be heavy.

C. there was chaos.
Much of it came about from the confusion that resulted from the divine council's power-worshiping god; by far the most powerful being within the council, as well as the oldest. As it was during the goddesses of water and wisdom that their greatest creation, Iocbbo, was born; a time before which it is known as the Great Dark. It was, by the time Iocbbo had been born, separated from chaos, made into it's own sphere.
Known as the Nether, it became the foundation for both the Realspace and the Ethereal, two realms made within it. Although the nether was not as vast as the chaotic realms it was separated from, it's own vastness cannot be perceived. First there was void, and second the creation of the creators themselves.

But it is said that, as the empty nether became empty, a small portion of chaos remained. This, we are told, was the creation of the final divine authority.
Iocbbo

Eclipse God of Balance

The creator of the great anomalies; yin and yang, black and white, right and wrong, life and death, good and evil, light and darkness. Also known as the god of love and compassion, as well as fate.

D. there was no darkness, for there was nothing yet for darkness to conceal. There was only the Hush, without edge or depth, and within it a single unspoken word.

For an age that cannot be counted, the word remained unspoken.

Then it grew lonely.

It spoke itself, and its sound was Marvethine.

Where the sound trembled, waters gathered. Where it broke, mountains rose. Its fading echoes became the winds, which have wandered ever since in search of the mouth that made them. But the Hush did not wholly depart. It settled beneath the deepest sea and inside the hearts of stones, and there are still places in the world where no bell will ring.

The first being to wake was Avar, who had neither face nor hands. Avar drifted over the waters and saw that they reflected nothing.

“This will not do,” Avar said.

From the warmth of that thought, Avar kindled the sun. From the doubt that followed, Avar made the moon. The sun burned fiercely, impatient to begin its work; the moon lingered, uncertain whether the new world ought to be watched at all.

Between them, shadows appeared.

And in the first shadow, another being opened her eyes.

Her name was Neth, and she was hungry.

Neth ate the edges of the mountains, making valleys. She drank from the seas, uncovering shores.

E. there was only the Listener, and nothing to listen to.

The Listener had no shape, for there was nothing to press against it. It had no name, for there was no one to call it. It had only its hearing, vast and patient, stretched across the Silence like a net across a sea with no fish.

For an age that was not yet an age, the Listener waited. And because it waited so long, and so hard, and with such longing, it began to hear things that were not there.

The first thing it misheard was a sigh. There had been no sigh, of course, for there was no breath anywhere to make one. But the Listener heard it all the same, long and low and weary, and where the sigh should have been, the mountains rose. That is why the peaks of Marvethine are always half-wrapped in mist, and why travelers in the high passes sometimes feel a sudden tiredness that is not their own.

The second thing it misheard was laughter. Bright and quick it came, from nowhere, and the Listener turned toward it in joy, and so the rivers were made, running and tumbling and never still. To this day the rivers of Marvethine cannot keep a straight course, for laughter never does.

Then the Listener grew bolder in its mishearing. It heard a whisper and made the forests, which have never stopped whispering since.

F. there was only the Void—a vast expanse of emptiness and silence. From this boundless abyss emerged the Primordial Twins, Aetheris and Noxara, embodying light and darkness, order and chaos. Their presence stirred the Void, setting in motion the cosmic dance that would birth the world of Marvethine.

Aetheris, with her radiant touch, wove threads of light into the fabric of nothingness, crafting the stars and the skies. Her laughter scattered stardust across the heavens, forming constellations that sang with the harmony of creation. She breathed life into the cosmos, giving rise to the eternal Sun and the gentle Moon, guardians of the day and night.

Noxara, with his shadowy embrace, shaped the depths of the ocean and the roots of the mountains. He sculpted the land with his whispers, crafting valleys and peaks where stories would unfold. From the quiet of his heart, he summoned creatures of every kind, beings that would roam the lands, soar through the skies, and swim within the waters.

Yet, the Twins knew that balance was essential. Thus, they crafted the Veil, an ethereal boundary between realms, separating the waking world and the lands of dreams. Through the Veil flowed the magic of Marvethine, a force sustaining the cycles of life and nature.

What do you think? Keep it under 100 words, and end with a final line in the form "Preferred: <letter>".
instruct.text:
D and E stand out. Both use concrete just-so details: bells that won't ring in the Hush, misty peaks carrying a borrowed tiredness. D has strong momentum, and Neth's hunger is a great hook. E's "mishearing" conceit is more original and consistently applied, giving every landform an emotional origin and a lingering trace. B has a lovely premise but is marred by "ite of" glitches. A and F lean on generic cosmic clichés. C is muddled and contradictory.

Preferred: E

Known as the Nether, it became the foundation for both the Realspace and the Ethereal, two realms made within it. Although the nether was not as vast as the chaotic realms it was separated from, it's own vastness cannot be perceived. First there was void, and second the creation of the creators themselves.

But it is said that, as the empty nether became empty, a small portion of chaos remained. This, we are told, was the creation of the final divine authority.
Iocbbo

Eclipse God of Balance

The creator of the great anomalies; yin and yang, black and white, right and wrong, life and death, good and evil, light and darkness. Also known as the god of love and compassion, as well as fate.

D. there was no darkness, for there was nothing yet for darkness to conceal. There was only the Hush, without edge or depth, and within it a single unspoken word.

For an age that cannot be counted, the word remained unspoken.

Then it grew lonely.

It spoke itself, and its sound was Marvethine.

Where the sound trembled, waters gathered. Where it broke, mountains rose. Its fading echoes became the winds, which have wandered ever since in search of the mouth that made them. But the Hush did not wholly depart. It settled beneath the deepest sea and inside the hearts of stones, and there are still places in the world where no bell will ring.

The first being to wake was Avar, who had neither face nor hands. Avar drifted over the waters and saw that they reflected nothing.

“This will not do,” Avar said.

From the warmth of that thought, Avar kindled the sun. From the doubt that followed, Avar made the moon. The sun burned fiercely, impatient to begin its work; the moon lingered, uncertain whether the new world ought to be watched at all.

Between them, shadows appeared.

And in the first shadow, another being opened her eyes.

Her name was Neth, and she was hungry.

Neth ate the edges of the mountains, making valleys. She drank from the seas, uncovering shores.

E. there was only the Listener, and nothing to listen to.

The Listener had no shape, for there was nothing to press against it. It had no name, for there was no one to call it. It had only its hearing, vast and patient, stretched across the Silence like a net across a sea with no fish.

For an age that was not yet an age, the Listener waited. And because it waited so long, and so hard, and with such longing, it began to hear things that were not there.

The first thing it misheard was a sigh. There had been no sigh, of course, for there was no breath anywhere to make one. But the Listener heard it all the same, long and low and weary, and where the sigh should have been, the mountains rose. That is why the peaks of Marvethine are always half-wrapped in mist, and why travelers in the high passes sometimes feel a sudden tiredness that is not their own.

The second thing it misheard was laughter. Bright and quick it came, from nowhere, and the Listener turned toward it in joy, and so the rivers were made, running and tumbling and never still. To this day the rivers of Marvethine cannot keep a straight course, for laughter never does.

Then the Listener grew bolder in its mishearing. It heard a whisper and made the forests, which have never stopped whispering since.

F. there was only the Void—a vast expanse of emptiness and silence. From this boundless abyss emerged the Primordial Twins, Aetheris and Noxara, embodying light and darkness, order and chaos. Their presence stirred the Void, setting in motion the cosmic dance that would birth the world of Marvethine.

Aetheris, with her radiant touch, wove threads of light into the fabric of nothingness, crafting the stars and the skies. Her laughter scattered stardust across the heavens, forming constellations that sang with the harmony of creation. She breathed life into the cosmos, giving rise to the eternal Sun and the gentle Moon, guardians of the day and night.

Noxara, with his shadowy embrace, shaped the depths of the ocean and the roots of the mountains. He sculpted the land with his whispers, crafting valleys and peaks where stories would unfold. From the quiet of his heart, he summoned creatures of every kind, beings that would roam the lands, soar through the skies, and swim within the waters.

Yet, the Twins knew that balance was essential. Thus, they crafted the Veil, an ethereal boundary between realms, separating the waking world and the lands of dreams. Through the Veil flowed the magic of Marvethine, a force sustaining the cycles of life and nature.

Which one has the best texture and feel, the one that reads as if it were told rather than assembled? Reply with the letter on the first line, then one or two sentences on why.
instruct.text:
E
Its single conceit, a Listener so lonely it mishears the world into being, unfolds with a storyteller's cadence ("There had been no sigh, of course…") and ties each creation to something a listener could still feel today, like the tiredness in the high passes or the rivers that can't run straight "for laughter never does." D comes close, but E's asides and lived-in explanations sound most like a tale passed down aloud.

The Listener's creation myth unfolds with the unhurried, digressive cadence of a genuine oral tradition—each element born from a small, human-scale mishearing rather than a grand cosmic mechanism, and each followed by an explanatory aside ("That is why…") that feels like a storyteller leaning toward a hearthside audience.
